title: Scope to tool with a human in the loop (CIBA HITL)
lede: One login, one token exchange, one approval. The OBO token keeps the full scope set; Authorize denies a write with a CIBA identifier, the gateway rewrites the 403 into a JSON-RPC 2.0 error, the human approves, the agent replays, Authorize permits.

steps.title: User initiates login
steps.what: The user opens the application in a browser and starts logging in. Nothing agent-specific has happened yet.
steps.why: Everything after this hangs off one login session. The user logs in once, not once per tool.

steps.title: Authorize request
steps.what: The application sends an OIDC authorization request to IAM Core for the client agentClient, asking for all three scopes at once.
steps.why: This is the only scope consent in the flow: the user consents once, up front, not per tool call.

steps.title: User authenticates
steps.what: The user authenticates with IAM Core. The arrow is two-way because the browser is redirected to IAM Core and returned afterwards.
steps.why: This proves who the human is. Password, MFA and similar steps are whatever policy requires.

steps.title: User token
steps.what: IAM Core returns a user token to the application.
steps.why: The audience is the API gateway, not the AI gateway. The exchange in step 7 changes the audience. The token already carries all three scopes.

steps.title: Agent authenticates
steps.what: The agent authenticates to IAM Core as itself, using its own non-human identity.
steps.why: The agent gets an identity separate from the user. That separation lets the OBO token say "this user, acting through this agent".

steps.title: Agent token
steps.what: IAM Core returns an agent token.
steps.why: It proves who the agent is, but names no user. It is never used on its own to call tools: it becomes the actor token in step 7.

steps.title: Token exchange: actor + user token
steps.what: Token exchange with the actor token (agent) and the user token (subject). The result is the OBO token. Two-way: the agent sends the request and gets the new token back.
steps.why: This is the only token exchange in the whole flow. The OBO token carries the FULL scope set; the token does not narrow per tool. Authorize does that.

steps.title: Write request
steps.what: The application asks the agent to do something that needs a write, for example "update this record".
steps.why: The agent, not the application, decides which tool to call.

steps.title: Write tool call
steps.what: The agent calls the write tool through the MCP Gateway, carrying the OBO token.
steps.why: The gateway sits in front of the MCP Server and intercepts the call before it reaches the tool.

steps.title: Policy decision request
steps.what: The gateway asks Authorize for a decision. The inputs are the user (sub), the agent (act), the tool and the action.
steps.why: The decision is made on who the user and agent are and which tool is called, not on token scopes alone. Authorize can plug into any gateway.

steps.title: 403 with identifier
steps.what: Policy says write requires HITL. Authorize triggers CIBA and returns DENY with an identifier, as an HTTP 403.
steps.why: The identifier ties the later replay (step 15) to this approval. Because Authorize starts the CIBA request, it holds the audit record.

steps.title: JSON-RPC 2.0 error with identifier
steps.what: The gateway rewrites the 403 into a JSON-RPC 2.0 error that carries the identifier, and returns it to the agent.
steps.why: SDKs that treat a raw 403 as fatal would kill the session. A JSON-RPC error looks like an ordinary tool error, so the session survives.

steps.title: Prompt for CIBA acceptance
steps.what: The agent sees the identifier and asks the application to prompt the user for CIBA acceptance.
steps.why: The agent never calls CIBA endpoints itself. It only relays the request to the application. This is the one custom behaviour the customer AI team writes.

steps.title: Accept / Yes
steps.what: The user accepts. The application tells the agent "yes".
steps.why: This is the human-in-the-loop moment. Approval is recorded against the CIBA request, not trusted from the agent word.

steps.title: Replay tool call, header has identifier
steps.what: The agent replays the same tool call with the same OBO token, adding a header that contains the identifier.
steps.why: This is how the approval context gets back to Authorize across the gateway. The agent only echoes the identifier.

steps.title: Policy decision request
steps.what: The gateway sends Authorize a second policy decision request, now including the identifier header.
steps.why: Same inputs as step 10, plus the identifier.

steps.title: Permit
steps.what: Authorize detects the header and checks the CIBA call. The human approved it, so Authorize returns PERMIT.
steps.why: The agent is not asked to prove the approval: Authorize verifies it. A denied or expired request is denied again.

steps.title: Tool request with OBO token
steps.what: The gateway forwards the tool request to the MCP Server with the OBO token.
steps.why: The MCP Server sees the user in sub and the agent in act, so downstream audit shows both.

steps.title: MCP Server executes the write
steps.what: The MCP Server calls the Resource Server to do the actual work.
steps.why: The write only happens after a human approved it.

steps.title: Resource Server result returns to MCP Server
steps.what: The Resource Server returns its result to the MCP Server.
steps.why: The result is data, not a token: nothing here widens what the agent can do next.

steps.title: Response inspected at Authorize
steps.what: As drawn, the MCP Server response goes to Authorize on its way back, not straight to the gateway.
steps.why: Probably response inspection or audit. The policy engine sees both directions of the call.

steps.title: Authorized response reaches the Gateway
steps.what: Authorize passes the response to the gateway.
steps.why: The gateway relays it to the caller.

steps.title: Gateway returns the result to the Agent
steps.what: The gateway returns the response to the agent.
steps.why: The agent sees an ordinary tool result.

steps.title: Agent shows the result in the Application
steps.what: The agent returns the result to the application, and the user sees it. Done.
steps.why: One login, one exchange, one approval: the write happened under the user identity with the agent recorded.
